cells.tense: The exchange runs both ways now, and you're at the table with your hands open.
cells.act: give one thing and take one thing, in balance
cells.ask: This week, hand a friend something small — time, an answer — and then let what they offer back land. Both directions, once, no deflecting it.
cells.core:
You can sit with someone and feel what they feel without turning into them. Being near another person and staying level with them is not common — you can get lost in their state or put a wall up, and you've found the line between. What you carried through your changes still holds, and it shows most plainly in the space between you and other people.

So let one exchange run both ways this week. Hand something over to someone close and let something come back when it's offered, instead of turning it away. Take it at the size it comes. Fairness moves through your hands when you let it, and the receiving is the side with rust on it.

cells.tense: You'll be guarding what's between you before it's happened, bracing for a fracture that hasn't come.
cells.act: let yourself be drawn before you choose
cells.ask: Before you decide how to handle someone this week, sit with what you might feel about them — the unfinished muddle, no verdict — for a full day first.
cells.core:
What you've built with the people close to you is solid, and it stands. But the guarding has gotten out in front of the feeling. A small strain arrives and you're already shoring the walls, checking whether the bond is still what it was — before anything has actually threatened it. The person on the other side meets the bracing, not you.

Let the pull arrive before the plan does. Choose one person, and for a day just feel what could be felt with them — mixed, unfinished, no fixing — and let yourself be drawn before you choose. The bond you've made can take a day of not being managed.

cells.tense: You stood at the door of the room with the people in it, and stayed outside it.
cells.act: gather your determination and hold the line
cells.ask: Find what you actually want with someone near you — a call returned, a habit changed, a question asked — and keep that heading once, when someone pushes against it.
cells.core:
Being close to people used to move you, and something in you still knows the way. But the connection you'd have felt has gone quiet, and you keep things smooth from a distance, where nobody gets near enough to disagree. What remains between you and others is held from outside it, not from within.

Determination isn't a mood; it's a heading you keep. Find the thing you want with someone close — a call returned, a habit changed, a question asked — and when the next push comes against it, hold that line once. Defend nothing else. That heading is what you're giving back, and the door you've been standing outside of opens from where you are.

cells.tense: The space between the people near you stays warm and level, and your own account says you had no hand in it.
cells.act: let the structure act instead of announcing it
cells.ask: Next time a dispute starts near you, hear all of it through before you touch it — no smoothing, no word in the middle. Just once, and watch what shifts.
cells.core:
You walk into a gathering and the temperature settles. A word here, a seat moved there, and what was about to tip rights itself. This steadiness has a keeper. Ask you, though, and you merely happened to be standing there.

Try one thing instead of the move. Next time it starts, take it all in before you do anything — the part you step over will come through, and you'll notice yourself stepping over it. Nothing has to change around you. The one doing this can start to see how it's done, from inside. That work has your fingerprints on it, whatever your story says.
cells.sheetLine: The calm between them is yours, and your story isn't.

attempts.check: The claim I can't fully support is that others notice this person holding things together while they say otherwise — the record states the 'Steward' mechanism, but nobody's notice is given, so the core only says the keeper's own account of themselves is a bystander's, never that anyone else sees it. A reader could reasonably say they genuinely aren't holding anything together, just watching; so the ask is built to be harmless even then — it only asks them to listen all the way through once before doing the thing they'd normally do, which costs nothing if the read is wrong. The sentence that serves me more than them is any version of 'you are the one who keeps the peace' as a verdict; I kept it as a description of one moment they could recognise, not a role handed to them.
